instagram.caption: Childcare in Boulder County costs $20,000 a year. For Longmont's median household income of $86K, that's a third of take-home pay. On this week's election special with Shakeel Dalal, we break down ballot measure 1A and why it matters. Full episode link in bio.

facebook.post: We sat down with Shakeel Dalal for an election special this week, and the numbers on Boulder County's ballot measure 1A are stark: childcare runs about $20,000 a year here. With Longmont's median household income at $86,000, that's a third of your take-home pay going to keep one child in care. As Brady jokes in this clip, some families are literally planning pregnancies on a five-year schedule so they only pay for one kid at a time. Measure 1A would raise property taxes by roughly $100 per year for the average home and subsidize childcare for families earning up to $150K. For some people, the math of working versus staying home just doesn't add up right now. If you're a parent in Longmont or Boulder County, how are you navigating childcare costs?

instagram.caption: Cut taxes on 99% of Coloradans and still raise $2.7 billion for schools? That's the math behind Amendment 87. On this week's Election Special with Shakeel Dalal, we broke down how it works. Full episode link in bio.

facebook.post: On this week's Election Special episode with Shakeel Dalal, we walked through Amendment 87, a Colorado ballot measure that lowers income taxes for anyone making under $1 million a year and raises them for those above that line. The result? An estimated $2.7 billion per year set aside for education and Medicaid. It's a counterintuitive piece of policy: cut taxes on nearly everyone, yet still generate billions more in revenue because the top earners carry so much of the total income. Have you already voted on 87, or are you still making up your mind?

He wishes he could vote yes. But the problem, as he puts it, is the arms race: if only one side disarms, the other has every incentive to gerrymander harder. It's a genuinely painful tension between principle and strategy, and the ensuing debate with Annie is worth the listen. facebook.post: On this week's election special with Shakeel Dalal, we broke down Boulder County Question 200, which would expand the county commission from three members to five. The scale problem is striking: Longmont's $500 million budget is overseen by seven city council members, while Boulder County's $1 billion budget is run by just three commissioners. And according to Shakeel, those three commissioners can't work together—they actually hate each other, which has led to real governance problems. When two out of three people have to agree on everything and those three people are at odds, you get dysfunction. The measure would add two more voices to the table. Do you think a bigger commission would improve how Boulder County operates, or does it just add more bureaucracy?
